theorems.name: Uniform Limit Theorem
theorems.statement: If f_n \to f uniformly on S and each f_n is continuous on S, then f is continuous on S.
theorems.conditions: Uniform (not merely pointwise) convergence is essential.
theorems.intuition: For large n, f and f_n are everywhere close, so f_n's continuity 'transfers' to f with only a small uniform error.
theorems.proofSketch: Three-epsilon argument: bound |f(x)-f(x0)| by |f(x)-f_n(x)| + |f_n(x)-f_n(x0)| + |f_n(x0)-f(x0)|, each term < \varepsilon/3.
theorems.example: f_n(x)=x^n on [0,1] fails to converge uniformly, and indeed the limit is discontinuous.
theorems.examReady: Uniform convergence + continuity of each f_n \Rightarrow continuity of the limit.

theorems.name: Weierstrass M-test
theorems.statement: If |f_n(x)| \le M_n for all x \in S and \sum M_n converges, then \sum f_n(x) converges uniformly (and absolutely) on S.
theorems.conditions: The bound M_n must not depend on x.
theorems.intuition: A convergent numerical series of bounds forces the tail of the function series to be uniformly small everywhere at once.
theorems.proofSketch: Apply the Cauchy criterion: partial sum differences are bounded by tail sums of \sum M_n, which vanish independent of x.
theorems.example: \sum \cos(nx)/n^2 converges uniformly on R via M_n = 1/n^2.

theorems.name: Banach Fixed-Point Theorem
theorems.statement: If (X,d) is a non-empty complete metric space and T:X\to X satisfies d(Tx,Ty)\le k\,d(x,y) for some k\in[0,1), then T has a unique fixed point in X.
theorems.conditions: Completeness of X is essential; k must be strictly less than 1.
theorems.intuition: Iterating T from any starting point produces a Cauchy sequence that (by completeness) must converge to a fixed point.
theorems.proofSketch: Show x_0,Tx_0,T^2x_0,\dots is Cauchy using the geometric decay from the contraction constant, then use completeness.
theorems.example: T(x)=x/2 on (0,1] is a contraction with no fixed point, since (0,1] is not complete.
theorems.examReady: Verify X complete, T a genuine contraction (k<1), conclude unique fixed point.
